Maladaptive Strategies.value: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
I am permanently an outsider now

vignette: When Maria Hernandez, a 68‑year‑old Arab American prison guard, walked into the southern wing of the facility on a humid July afternoon, she was still haunted by the night three years earlier when a violent altercation broke out between two inmates. She had been standing near the corridor’s narrow window, trying to keep her training manual out of reach when one of the men shoved a knife into her chest. The blade slipped but she did not feel the cold metal; instead she saw the victim’s face, the blood spattering the white wall, and her own body go rigid with terror before she could even think about screaming. The shock fractured her sense of safety and, for months afterward, the memory of that knife and the echo of that blood‑stained scream became a constant background hum in her mind. She now wakes each night with the sound of the prison’s silence pressing against her chest, as if the air itself were a weapon. Sleep eludes her; she tosses and turns, hearing faint whispers of footsteps that never materialize, and she finds herself racing through the halls in her mind long before the first guard’s flashlight flickers on. Maria’s self‑reported symptoms coalesce into a tight, self‑reinforcing loop. Her negative appraisals—“I should have protected the other inmates; I failed,” “I am permanently an outsider now,” and “People can’t be trusted”—form the core of the story that drives her day‑to‑day life. Because she believes she has let others into danger, she feels the need to keep herself surrounded by people so she never has to face her thoughts alone. That constant socialising—her “maladaptive strategy” of staying in the break room while her coworkers chat and laugh—does not alleviate her fear; it only makes her feel more exposed. The belief that she cannot protect anyone fuels a heightened sense of threat; she watches every flicker of movement, every distant shout, and her body reacts before her mind can calm her. In turn, the persistent threat she feels pushes her to drop responsibilities at work, such as declining to take the night shift or refusing to stand guard at a high‑risk cell. By giving up these duties she believes she is keeping herself and others safer, yet this avoidance only confirms her sense of failure and her outsider status. The cycle loops again when she, in a moment of heightened vigilance, misinterprets a quiet hallway as a potential ambush and, in panic, steps back, reinforcing her mistrust of those around her. Her constant checking of surroundings—an extension of the same maladaptive strategy—keeps her in a state of perpetual readiness, and the effort itself stokes the threat perception she had already convinced herself she cannot escape. Each action, whether socialising or retreating, deepens her conviction that she failed and that she is permanently unsafe. Because Maria’s daily environment is the prison, her triggers are woven into the fabric of her work. When she walks through the quiet cells at night, the sudden stillness makes her heart pound, and the body’s automatic fight response surges before she can even consider calling a guard. She often leaves her shift early, citing exhaustion, and then spends the rest of the evening alone in the staff lounge, where she scrolls through news articles about prison violence, hoping a news story will remind her of the dangers she thinks she has already survived. Her spouse, who worries that Maria is withdrawing, has suggested counseling, but Maria insists she cannot “trust anyone else to understand the real danger” that she believes constantly lurks in the walls. The fear that she will be caught in another violent act keeps her from even talking about her feelings at home, leaving her feeling more isolated than ever. After months of escalating avoidance, a supervisor noticed Maria’s consistent lateness for training and her tendency to avoid paperwork, labeling her as “inconsistent.” Maria’s body reacts before her mind as she feels the weight of a reprimand—her heart racing, her fingers tightening on the pen—yet she avoids the meeting, convinced that her failure will lead to a reprimand she cannot handle. The avoidance only makes the reprimand seem more imminent, and the cycle of fear, avoidance, and negative appraisal tightens further. Over time, the threat she feels in even ordinary moments—like a sudden silence in a busy corridor—has made her sleep fragmented, and she no longer can find peace at home. She now seeks help, afraid that without intervention she will be unable to protect herself and her loved ones, hoping instead to regain a sense of control and trust in the world that has, for years, felt like a hostile arena.
